transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Hannah Cole (Redwood CSM), Priya Nair (Verdant Head of ML), Omar Sadiq (Verdant Infra), Sofia Martinez (Verdant Product), Kenji Yamauchi (Verdant SRE)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC sync focused on throughput tuning results from last sprint, discussion of continuous batching vs concurrency targets, reconciling latency SLOs with cost, and agreeing a "fallthrough" plan when dedicated capacity is saturated. Action items and next steps captured at end.

Topics covered:
- Results from last burst-run (3x short bursts) and steady-state run
- Continuous batching impact on p50/p90 for Verdant request shapes
- Queueing/backpressure and client-side throttles
- Concurrency targets and target SLOs (p95/p99 discussion)
- Fallthrough/fallback policy when dedicated pool is full (hosted variants)
- Security/VM/VPC notes and who needs to be involved

Notes / Links mentioned:
- Benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/bench/verdant-poc-benchmark (shared)
- Short demo recording from Diego (link posted in chat)
- Security doc: redwood.com/security/enterprise-overview (referenced)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena: ok, thanks everyone for joining, um we're on for 45 minutes, quick agenda, run through the numbers Diego did a few runs overnight, then dig into any tuning and the fallthrough plan, is that good?
[00:12] Priya: yes, sounds good. we've got a hard launch window in mid april so we want to lock the steady state targets this week ideally.
[00:20] Diego: quick note, the overnight run was two parts: a 10-minute steady-state at 256 concurrency and a 3x 2-minute burst to 768, we captured tail latencies and token costs per request. spreadsheet's in the link.
[00:35] Omar: I skimmed it quickly, some of the p90s spiked during the bursts, expected, but we need to understand whether batching or more concurrency is cheaper for us.
[00:44] Diego: right, at 256 steady we saw p50 around 110ms p90 ~240ms, token cost per call 0.014 units. During the 768 bursts p95 went up to 640ms, p99 1.2s but cost per token normalized went down slightly because of more contiguous KV cache hits.
[01:05] Priya: wait, you said KV cash hits? do you mean K-V cache?
[01:08] Diego: yes, sorry, K-V cache, automatic prefix caching kicked in during sustained bursts so decoder had fewer mem loads. transcription sometimes turns that into cash.
[01:18] Sofia: quick question — whats the user-visible latency target again? we talked p95 500ms earlier?
[01:24] Priya: our product goal is p95 <= 400ms for the QA path, but we accept p99 up to 1.1s for async flows.
[01:33] Lena: ok so there's a gap when bursts happen. two levers: increase concurrency (more pods / more dedicated GPU) or adjust batching (continuous batching to group more requests). both have tradeoffs for cost and SLO.
[01:47] Kenji: from infra side we prefer to avoid frequent autoscale because of cold-starts into VPC peering and KMS handshake times — that adds jitter.
[01:58] Omar: that was a concern: when we hit a cold scale up, the p99 jumps. can Redwood do warm standby?
[02:05] Diego: we can pre-warm reserved lanes (dedicated) and keep a small buffer of warm workers. also fallthrough to hosted variants in the same region as a last resort; there's a small cross-account billing trigger but it keeps user experience up.
[02:21] Priya: ok, we want a concrete fallthrough flow: prefer Dedicated -> Dedicated burst pool -> Hosted warm lane -> degradations (reduce max tokens)
[02:32] Lena: agreed. we'll propose a policy doc. Diego, can you outline the exact ordering and the cost implications?
[02:39] Diego: yes, I'll include cost delta per million tokens. example: Dedicated steady cost baseline X, burst lanes add +20% on reserved cost but reduce p95 by 40ms; hosted backup adds 8% per token but keeps latency within SLO most of the time. spreadsheet has numbers.
[02:58] Sofia: on batching, what's the difference between continuous batching and client-side aggregate batching?
[03:05] Diego: Continuous batching is server-side: the runtime groups incoming requests across client connections up to a max batch size or a time window. Client aggregation means the app waits to fill a batch then sends a single request. For Verdant's QA path with many short requests, continuous batching removes client complexity and yields better KV reuse. downside: it can add jitter for singletons.
[03:30] Priya: do we lose determinism with continuous batching? some of our tests expect ordered token diffs.
[03:36] Diego: the model output is identical; only latency distribution changes. ordering and decoding are same. any non-determinism comes from sampling; we didn't change seeds.
[03:46] Kenji: security question: if we fallthrough to hosted, does data leave our VPC? what about KMS keys for encryption at rest?
[03:54] Lena: good call — fallthrough will use a customer-scoped hosted variant with SOC2 controls; we still enforce encryption, but we need to agree on allowed data residency for fallthrough. we'll loop in security docs and legal.
[04:08] Omar: i'll need the exact KMS flow and whether keys are service-managed or customer-managed.
[04:12] Lena: noted, will schedule a KMS/VPC session. next step.
[04:18] Diego: back to numbers, i wanted to highlight continuous batching reduced mean tokens/sec overhead by 12% in the steady run, and boosted KV hit rate from 18% to 34% in burst. that explains lower token cost during bursts even though latency rises.
[04:36] Priya: so if we tuned batch timeout shorter, would that reduce p95?
[04:40] Diego: tradeoff: shorter timeout reduces queuing but lowers batch formation so cost per token increases. we can tune batch_timeout_ms and max_batch_size per route.
[04:50] Sofia: can we have different profiles per route? QA vs draft generation?
[04:54] Diego: yes, per-route config is supported. set QA to aggressive latency targets (low timeout, smaller max batch) and draft generation to cost-optimized (higher timeout, larger max batch).
[05:03] Priya: what's the best concurrency target for QA then? 256 felt ok but we need p95 at 400ms.
[05:09] Diego: short answer: push steady to 320-384 concurrency with slightly tighter batching (batch_timeout 12ms, max_batch 8) should hit p95 ~380ms in our sim. but we need to validate with Verdant traces.
[05:22] Lena: Diego, can you run a 1-hour validation at 320 concurrency with those batching params?
[05:27] Diego: yes, will run and share CSV.
[05:30] Omar: we'll provide traces by monday, is that fine?
[05:32] Priya: yes we'll anonymize and send.
[05:35] Diego: great. also note we saw memory pressure on one of the GPU lanes during a long burst; that might be caused by oversized context lengths in some requests.
[05:45] Priya: interesting, could be analytic requests that include full document context. we can reduce max_context for model calls to help.
[05:51] Kenji: on queueing/backpressure, does Redwood expose a token-level backlog or request queue metric we can integrate to our SRE alerts?
[05:58] Diego: yes, there are metrics: inflight_requests, batch_size_distribution, queue_latency_ms, and kv_cache_hit_rate. we can add custom tracing hooks for token-level breakdowns.
[06:10] Lena: Hannah from CSM — anything from your side on adoption or ramp?
[06:14] Hannah: just tracking success criteria: p95 <=400ms for QA, cost per 1M tokens not exceeding baseline +25% in steady state, and an agreed fallthrough policy. also want a runbook for SRE handoffs.
[06:27] Sofia: runbook would be great. can Redwood author a starter runbook?
[06:31] Lena: yes, we'll provide a draft runbook with escalation steps.
[06:34] Diego: another tuning note: we recommend controlling client concurrency cap so you don't flood the queue; a soft-throttle at client layer helps maintain SLOs.
[06:44] Omar: are there recommendations for our lambda-based workers? we have many short-lived containers calling the API.
[06:49] Diego: for lambda, prefer connection pooling and warm concurrency; increase reserved concurrency per function to smooth peaks, and implement exponential backoff with jitter on retries.
[06:58] Priya: ok, about the fallthrough policy, can we sketch an explicit example flow?
[07:03] Lena: example: if dedicated pool reaches 85% sustained for 30s -> spin burst lanes up to 50% capacity -> if 90th percentile still > SLA and incoming qps > threshold -> route low-priority requests (draft gen) to hosted lane; if still overloaded -> reduce max_tokens for non-critical endpoints.
[07:20] Kenji: timeline: mid april launch means we need final run this week and one final validation two weeks out.
[07:27] Lena: agreed. we should also capture cost vs latency curves for CFO review. Diego can produce a two-column CSV.
[07:34] Diego: yes, I'll add cost per million tokens at each concurrency/batch setting.
[07:38] Priya: any blockers from security?
[07:40] Lena: not blockers but items: KMS ownership for fallthrough, VPC peering timing, and SOC2 evidence for hosted variant. we'll share security doc and schedule a session.
[07:51] Omar: one more infra question: do you support pinned model versions during fallthrough? we can't have model drifts.
[07:58] Diego: yes, model pinning is supported and the fallthrough will use the same model binary where available; if exact binary isn't available in hosted, we route to a validated semantically-equivalent variant. we'll document any subtle diffs.
[08:12] Sofia: can we get a small A/B test for fallthrough to measure user impact?
[08:15] Lena: yes, propose 5% traffic for fallthrough for 24h and collect quality/latency metrics.
[08:21] Priya: good. we'll need to annotate traces for A/B.
[08:24] Diego: ok I'll include A/B flags in the benchmark tool.
[08:29] Lena: let's review the concrete runs Diego will perform and dates.
[08:33] Diego: plan: run 1 - 1hr at 320 concurrency with batch_timeout 12ms, max_batch 8 (steady). run 2 - 3x 2min bursts to 768 (burst-run). run 3 - 1hr at 256 with client-side soft throttle to compare. I'll post CSVs by 2026-04-02.
[08:52] Priya: 2026-04-02 works. Omar will upload traces by 2026-04-05.
[08:58] Kenji: can we get a short doc mapping Redwood metrics to our SRE alert names?
[09:02] Hannah: we'll produce a mapping doc after Diego posts metrics.
[09:07] Sofia: any rough numbers on expected incremental monthly cost for burst lanes?
[09:10] Diego: rough: burst lanes add 5-12% depending on utilization. i'll send concrete ranges in the pricing sheet.
[09:18] Priya: ok, last question: what's the fallback when model variant mismatch occurs during fallthrough? degrade gracefully?
[09:24] Diego: two options: if semantically equivalent variant exists we route; otherwise we fall back to a cached response or return a degraded mode with a warning header to client. prefer route to equivalent variant.
[09:35] Lena: cool. let's capture action items.
[09:38] Priya: can we also get a short runbook for troubleshooting p99 spikes?
[09:42] Lena: yes, Diego will include triage steps.
[09:46] Transcript quality notes: automatic transcription had a few mislabels (K-V cache -> K-V cash), speaker overlaps once around 00:20.

Recap / Action items (as read out):
- Diego: run validation runs (320 steady, bursts to 768, 256 throttle compare) and post CSV + cost curves - due 2026-04-02
- Omar: upload anonymized 48h request traces to shared drive - due 2026-04-05
- Lena: send updated pricing sheet and draft fallthrough policy doc - due 2026-04-01
- Redwood Security (Lena + Security) to schedule KMS/VPC session with Verdant infra - target week of 2026-04-06
- Hannah: draft SRE runbook & metric mapping after Diego's metrics are posted - due 2026-04-04

Close: meeting ends ~15:46 PT. thanks everyone.

Additional freeform notes (misc):
- Verdant accepted the idea of a 5% A/B fallthrough test to quantify user impact.
- Diego flagged a potential memory pressure case tied to long contexts; Verdant to optionally limit max_context in the client for hotspots.
- Competitors mentioned during conversation as comparators for hosted fallback: Anthropic, Vertex AI, Cohere.

End of transcript.
